headline: Expects RBA to hike in September but hold in November; core inflation still running hot is the key risk
reasoning: Will Banks expects the RBA to raise rates in September but does not anticipate a follow-up hike in November, viewing back-to-back hikes as overly aggressive. He notes that headline inflation is trending down in line with the RBA's target band, which supports a pause after a September move. However, he flags that core/underlying inflation — stripping out volatile items like petrol and food — remains persistently elevated, which is the central bank's primary concern. He believes a November hike would face significant internal and external objection.
quote: I think that they would increase them in September. I think they would want to see how that played out. I think to do it in September, increase them again in November, I think would be. I think that would be pretty aggressive. Um, and like I said, the inflation is the headline. Inflation is coming down. Um, which is, which is which is what they want. So therefore it is coming down. And therefore by pushing that rate up a bit, it is going to push it further in terms of it coming down within that line, in that range that they want to, uh, they want inflation to sit within. Um, the issue that they've got though is, um, it is the it's the underlying core inflation drivers. So when you remove things like volatile stuff like petrol, food, stuff like that, it's the core inflation that sits there consistently, which is still sitting fairly hot, fairly strong. Um, and that is their issue. So I don't think they would increase it in November. I would be surprised if they did that. I think there would be a lot of objection.
episode_title: The RBA’s September reckoning

headline: Expects RBA to hike 25bp in September to 4.6%, driven by persistent household spending and sticky inflation above the 2–3% target band
reasoning: Will Banks argues that inflation remains too high (CPI at 3.8%, above the 2–3% target), household spending has increased consecutively in May, June and July (July +1.1%), and the RBA's own August meeting notes signalled readiness to raise rates again. He also notes that if the RBA skips September, the next meeting is November, risking further entrenchment of inflation. He believes a 25bp hike to 4.6% is likely, with a pause in November to assess the impact.
quote: I see there being sort of key three key areas. So the first one, if we look at the indicators. So inflation is not coming down quickly enough. It still remains pretty strong. Household spending is increasing. It was 1.1% in July. Um that had increased in May and June. Um, we've got therefore this demand is still there for spending and it's not it isn't slowing down. Um, so this is affecting the headline inflation of the of the CPI, which has fallen to 3.8, but it's still not where it needs to be between 2 to 3%... I believe they will increase it to about 4.6%. So 25 basis points.
episode_title: The RBA’s September reckoning

headline: Weak AUD risk if inflation not controlled: could trigger larger wage demands, more expensive imports and prolonged rate rises in a feedback loop
reasoning: Will Banks flags that if the RBA fails to bring inflation under control, a weaker Australian dollar is a key risk, as it would make imports more expensive, fuel wage demand, and ultimately push inflation higher again, requiring longer and larger rate increases. This feedback loop is identified as a core concern motivating a September hike.
quote: The fact that, you know, property prices are slowing down, but they're still 50% higher than the where they were six years ago. Um, so that's what the issue is, is the fact that they are concerned that if they don't get on top of this, it could land up, weakening the dollar. Um, imports become more expensive. You're going to have larger wage increased demands because of that. You're going to have more, uh, and longer interest rate increases. It's going to push up inflation again.
episode_title: The RBA’s September reckoning

headline: Dismisses overtightening risk: recession threat stems from energy, insurance and property shortages, not RBA alone; one hike then hold expected
reasoning: Will Banks acknowledges the 'damned if you do, damned if you don't' dilemma, conceding that overtightening is the strongest counter-argument. However, he believes the spending trajectory (rising for three consecutive months) makes inaction riskier. He also argues that a potential recession would not be solely attributable to the RBA given structural cost pressures from energy, insurance and housing. He does not expect a follow-up hike in November if September proceeds, seeing that sequence as too aggressive.
quote: They're a little bit kind of damned if they do, damned if they don't. And that is one of the strongest arguments against the September increase is that there's a concern that are they pushing it too far. Is it really going to kick off a recession?... At the end of the day with, with them cutting in too much, if there's a recession, it's not just down to interest rates. Um, and down to the RBA, you're looking at energy price increases, insurance price increases, uh, you know, property shortages, etc.. So it's not just the RBA that will be potentially, um, uh, creating a risk of a recession.
episode_title: The RBA’s September reckoning

headline: Global long-term government borrowing costs rising as maturing bonds are refinanced at higher rates, compounding debt burdens
reasoning: Will Banks explains that globally, long-term government borrowing is rising because large volumes of older bonds are maturing and being refinanced at today's higher interest rates, increasing the cost of debt servicing. This creates a compounding dynamic where governments are borrowing more partly just to pay interest on existing debt, similar to the UK's approach of rolling debt forward. He distinguishes between productive capital expenditure borrowing (e.g. infrastructure) which generates an economic return, versus operational expenditure borrowing which does not and can be inflationary.
quote: What does it all mean? It means that we're not in a debt crisis, we've increased our borrowing. But at the end of the day, when you look at the whole global market, the long term borrowing of all governments is rising. And that's because a lot of these bonds are maturing, governments are having to issue new bonds. And at today's rates, there are higher interest rates. So that cost of the debt obligation has increased. And that is why governments are borrowing more partly as well, because they need to borrow to pay some of the interest.
episode_title: the COB: yield me a break

headline: Australia's gross government debt hits $1 trillion but net debt position remains relatively sound compared to G10 peers
reasoning: Will Banks from Challenger Capital notes that while Australia has crossed the $1 trillion gross debt mark, net debt is roughly half that figure after offsetting government financial assets. On a debt-to-GDP basis, Australia sits at around 34%, the best position among G10 countries, with Germany at around 64% and Japan at 237%. He acknowledges that interest payments are running at around $30 billion per year and are projected to rise to $43 billion by 2030, representing roughly $150 million per day. The key concern is the opportunity cost — rising debt servicing crowds out spending on hospitals, schools, and infrastructure, forcing higher taxes or further borrowing. He notes the current deficit of around $32 billion is stabilising and likely to decline over coming years.
quote: So yes, we've hit the $1 trillion mark of gross debt. But we are talking gross debt, not net debt, which offsets some of the government's financial assets. So if you're going to look at net debt, we're looking at about half of that... when you look at the recent stats of the IMS, at the moment, we're sitting at around about 34%. And when we compare that to the other G10 countries, we're actually in the best position, the worst being Japan, where they're at 237%... at the moment, we're looking at around about 30 billion a year on that. And by 2030, that will increase to about 43 billion. So that looks at around about 150 million a day in interest rate payments.

headline: Will Banks (Challenger Capital) warns Australian property prices will continue to drift lower, not rebound, as negative gearing changes and tighter lending weigh on demand.
reasoning: Banks argues that multiple headwinds are converging on the Australian property market: tighter lending standards restrict product availability and increase costs for borrowers; the removal of negative gearing on existing properties has hurt investor returns and now threatens capital growth expectations; developers face difficulty covering costs if forced to reduce prices; and a wealth-effect reversal is making consumers more cautious with spending, creating a potential vicious cycle of lower demand, business lay-offs, and rising unemployment. He does not expect prices to rebound quickly, instead forecasting a gradual drift downward over time. He advises buyers and investors to focus on fundamentals — affordability, repayment capacity under higher-for-longer rates, location — rather than fear of missing out.
quote: I think these prices are not going to shoot back up again for some time. If anything, I think they're going to drip down over time. You've got investors who have now lost negative gearing on existing properties. Now, what it looks like is they've now got an impact on their capital growth. You've got developers who have invested, may have difficulty trying to sell. Can they cover their costs if they're looking at bringing having to reduce price. And then you've also got those individuals and voters. So individually, could be facing issues such as people that own or working for furniture companies not selling as much, white goods manufacturers, those people and businesses that are dependent on individuals renovating their homes.
episode_title: Is the property market witnessing a healthy correction or severe downturn?

headline: Will Banks (Challenger Capital) characterises Australian housing decline as a healthy correction, not a crash, with Melbourne and Sydney leading a multi-factor downturn
reasoning: Banks describes Melbourne prices as approximately 5% below their peak, with monthly falls of around 0.7% since 2022 and national listings up 23% year-on-year (Melbourne up 43%). He attributes the correction to higher interest rates reducing borrowing capacity, stretched affordability after years of rapid price growth, and more cautious investors following federal budget changes to negative gearing. He distinguishes a correction from a crash, noting a crash would imply 30-40% falls, which is not occurring. He sees the correction continuing for some time but views it as a healthy affordability rebalancing that creates opportunities for those previously priced out.
quote: I would say that it's a healthy correction. Um, it is a correction of the price. So for me, a crash would really suggest a fall of around about 30 to 40% in prices, which is just not what's happening at the moment. Nowhere near that. Um, so really what we're finding is that the, the, um, the market is now adjusting and it's adjusting after many years of this rapid growth that's been created by interest rates, which have been extremely low. Um, so it is I see this as a correction. I think the correction is going to occur for some time. Uh, but I think what I really want to say is that price corrections aren't necessarily bad. What they actually do is they create affordability balancing in the market. And they actually do also create opportunities for those who have really been priced out of the market for many years and have been forced to continue to rent.
episode_title: Is the property market witnessing a healthy correction or severe downturn?

He also flags downstream economic effects on businesses tied to housing activity — furniture, white goods manufacturers, and renovation-dependent businesses — as potentially significant. He frames this as a politically complicated outcome with winners (first-home buyers, upgraders) and losers (recent peak buyers, investors, developers).

So I would say those people will be thinking, well, this is great that this is happening. But then there's the other side of it that those, as you just said, there's those people that have bought at a peak time, they're now in this neck of equity, which is not only bad on its own, it's the fact that if they've got a mortgage, you've then got tighter lives. Therefore, the amount of the type of products that they might be available to to them could be more expensive. You've got the investors who have now, uh, lost negative gearing on existing properties. Now, what it looks like is they've now got an impact on their capital growth. You've got developers who have invested, um, may have difficulty trying to sell. Can they cover their costs if they're looking at bringing having to reduce price.

headline: Will Banks flags negative wealth effect from falling house prices as a risk to consumer spending and broader business activity.
reasoning: Banks highlights that when property prices rise, even unrealised gains make homeowners feel wealthier and more inclined to spend. With prices now falling, consumer confidence is weakening and discretionary spending is contracting. This affects furniture retailers, white goods manufacturers, renovation-related businesses and broader consumer-facing industries. A pullback in consumer spending can in turn force businesses to reduce headcount, pushing up unemployment and creating a self-reinforcing negative feedback loop.
quote: During times where people feel more wealthier because their prices have probably gone up, even though it's not realized, they will go out and spend more. And now the prices have come down, they're more cautious, spending less, and therefore that affects businesses, people and incomes. Therefore, those people also may have an issue with the government and some of these decisions that are being taken. Particularly to talk about businesses who may see lower demand, they may be forced to lay off people. Unemployment rate rises. And so it goes.

headline: Will Banks warns changes to negative gearing on existing properties will create a two-tier housing market, pushing prices of new builds higher and pricing out lower-income buyers
reasoning: Banks explains that under the new negative gearing rules, only new builds can be negatively geared, which will drive investment dollars into new construction and inflate prices in that segment. Pre-existing homes purchased for investment or owner-occupation will lose that tax advantage, splitting the market. Wealthier investors with available capital will compete for new builds, driving those prices up, while those with less capital will be priced out entirely. He views this as creating inflation within the property market itself, contrary to the broader goal of bringing inflation down.
quote: What that's going to mean is, is that those investors that do have access funds that want to deploy into the property market. We'll be looking to put it into these new builds. And what that means is that those prices will go up, and those people that are maybe more restricted in terms of how much money they've got. They'll be priced out. So that's create that is creating kind of a like an inflation within that market itself.
episode_title: Investing after the era of "cheap money"

headline: Will Banks argues the era of cheap money is over for Australia, with higher rates structurally constraining household borrowing power and discretionary spending
reasoning: Banks notes that from 2009 to 2022, ultra-cheap money fuelled house prices and share markets, with one third of all Australian mortgages taken out during that period. Now that rates have risen significantly, the amount a family can borrow has fallen from ~$1 million to ~$750k, reducing purchasing power and increasing mortgage repayments and car loans. He argues this is creating a K-shaped economy where wealthier households are less affected because they may not need to borrow, while lower-income households bear the full brunt of rate increases. He is cautious that rate rises alone may not be effective if offset by minimum wage increases and ongoing government spending.
quote: For any context, from around 2009 to 2022, um, money in Australia was very cheap. Um, and it meant borrow cheaply, you could buy a home, it expand your business investments, etc.. Uh, and what is interesting is that during that time, one third of all Australian mortgages actually taken out. So it was ultra cheap money... if you look at $1 million in 2021, um, that's what a family could borrow. Now, if you look at what what that represents, the amount they could borrow now is around 750 K. And this is due to the fact that the interest rates have gone up. But it's also because of serviceability.
episode_title: Investing after the era of "cheap money"

headline: Will Banks argues RBA rate rises are being partially offset by minimum wage increases, creating a circular inflationary dynamic that limits the effectiveness of monetary tightening
reasoning: Banks contends that while higher interest rates aim to reduce spending and bring down inflation, concurrent increases in the minimum wage inject more money into the economy and counteract that goal. This circular dynamic means inflation is not being reduced as intended. He calls for rates to be held steady but urges careful coordination of other government policies so they do not undermine the inflation-fighting objective of monetary tightening.
quote: By increasing interest rates, you're trying to control spending to bring the inflation to bring inflation down. But because you've increased in interest rates things are more expensive. And therefore to counteract that the minimum wage has been increased. So you go around in a circle. So you therefore aren't really reducing inflation because there's more money floating around because people with minimum wages has been increased. So what does that mean? It means that you've got to increase inflation again. So I think we do need to keep interest rates where they are. But I think we need to be very careful with the policies that are also sitting alongside that, so that they don't essentially offset what we're trying to achieve by increasing interest rates.
episode_title: Investing after the era of "cheap money"
